value.overview: The Plain-colored Tanager (Tangara inornata) is a small, subdued tanager of the Caribbean lowlands of Central and northern South America. Its mostly gray or blue-gray plumage is relieved by darker wings and tail, a dark facial mask, and a small blue shoulder patch that can be difficult to see. It is a canopy and forest-edge bird, often overlooked because it lacks the bright colors of many related tanagers. Costa Rica marks the northern part of its distribution.
value.classification: The Plain-colored Tanager belongs to the tanager family Thraupidae and the genus Tangara. It is a passerine, or perching bird.
value.identification: Adults are mainly plain gray, blue-gray, or slate-colored, with darker wings and tail and a contrasting dark area around the face. A small blue patch on the shoulder is an important field mark, although it may be hidden when the wing is folded. The underparts are generally paler than the back. Males and females are similar in appearance. In Costa Rica, careful attention is needed because several other tanagers can appear grayish in poor light or from a distance.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from the Caribbean lowlands of southeastern Costa Rica through Panama to northern Colombia. In Costa Rica it is a localized resident of the humid Caribbean lowlands, especially the eastern and northeastern lowlands, including areas around Limón and northern Alajuela such as Boca Tapada. It uses humid lowland evergreen forest, forest edges, clearings with trees, tall second growth, and other partly disturbed habitats. It is most often encountered in the canopy or upper levels of vegetation.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered a resident species in Costa Rica and is not known for long-distance seasonal migration. Individuals may make local movements in response to food supplies or breeding conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding information specifically from Costa Rica is limited. Elsewhere in its range, the Plain-colored Tanager breeds during the local wet-season period, with breeding reported from about February to August in Panama. The female builds a small, concealed cup nest from plant fibers and cobwebs, while the male may help gather material and feed the young. Clutches commonly contain about two eggs. Nest placement and timing may vary with local rainfall and habitat conditions.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of small fruits and berries, supplemented by insects and other arthropods. It usually searches among foliage and branches in the forest canopy or at forest edges, picking food from vegetation. It may join mixed-species feeding flocks with other tanagers and small insect-eating birds, particularly where fruiting trees or productive patches of forest concentrate food.
value.behavior: Plain-colored Tanagers are generally active, alert birds that forage in pairs, small groups, or mixed-species flocks. They often remain high in trees, where their quiet colors and quick movements make them easy to miss. The species may use both relatively intact forest and disturbed areas with remaining trees. Its calls and behavior can be more useful for detection than plumage alone, especially in the dense lowland forests of eastern Costa Rica.

conservation.populationTrend: A precise global population estimate and dependable long-term trend are not available. The species has a broad distribution and remains locally present in suitable habitat, including protected and semi-protected areas of Costa Rica.
